extracted.intended_audience: general readers of humorous literary criticism; theatre/music enthusiasts
extracted.subtask_description: A humorous essay that comments on literature, theatre, opera, art markets, and social manners — giving evaluative observations about how art is made, received, and performed. Useful as informal guidance for writers, performers, and culturally literate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature is the art of make-believe
rubrics_metrics.description: “Literature is the art of make-believe.” The author ‘pretends’ characters and events, and the audience knowingly accepts the fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful literary work depends on the author inventing (making up) what will please the audience while maintaining an attitude of artistic necessity. The audience participates by consenting to the premise (e.g., paying for the story); without that participation the pretense would collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of disbelief / communal make-believe
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatre (and literature) rely on communal agreement to accept obvious contrivances (a wobbling thing as a castle, pushed ‘ocean’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers may use flimsy sets or conventional stage devices because the audience agrees to pretend. This is an acceptable theatrical economy: clarity and audience willingness to accept conventions matter more than literal realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial authenticity while entertaining
rubrics_metrics.description: The author must 'make-believe' that he cannot help but create (i.e., present the work as an act of art), yet craft what will please the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good writing balances evident invention with a convincing voice of necessity; overly self-conscious fabrication or transparent catering that breaks the pretense weakens the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opera: musical necessity often sacrifices natural acting
rubrics_metrics.description: In grand opera, musical requirements frequently override realistic acting (characters address the audience, sing while doing implausible physical actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an inherent convention — anti-patterns to avoid if naturalism is desired include having lovers turn to footlights to declare love, or expecting realistic physical interaction while performers sing at full voice. If aiming for believable drama, adapt staging and composition so voice and action align; if sticking to operatic convention, accept the trade-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between orchestra and singers
rubrics_metrics.description: Orchestration must not permanently drown the singer: a single woman struggling to be heard against a large orchestra is unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good musical drama considers dynamic balance; excessively powerful orchestral writing that consistently overpowers singers undermines the clarity and dramatic effect. Beware of repertoire or performances where orchestral mass routinely makes vocal lines inaudible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting should reflect realistic responses and stage business
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural acting involves appropriate, believable physical reactions (e.g., if a mob is at the door, characters should realistically push to barricade it rather than recite calmly apart).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When striving for believable theatre, consider the small practical details of behaviour — how people actually move, talk, and interact under stress — rather than relying on theatrical convention that separates singing/speaking from natural responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operatic convention as an unavoidable trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: Because singing demands physical and vocal economy, conventional operatic business (static positions, staged recitative to audience) is often required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept this as a feature rather than a flaw when writing or staging opera; experienced artists 'husband their resources' and occupy positions that preserve vocal production. For directors wanting more naturalism, find musical and staging compromises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality criteria for a chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal operatic chorus is experienced, united, sober, industrious, and musically knowledgeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good chorus exhibits unity of appearance and ensemble, avoids youthful giddiness, and relies on discipline and musical literacy. These attributes make the chorus a credible scenic element and improve overall production coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art-market reputation manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Dealers can create an artist's market value by arranging articles, controversy, and selective publicity, then selling to known buyers (the ‘American millionaire’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating art or an emerging artist, be aware of market-manufacturing tactics: press campaigns, planted anecdotes, strategic auctions, and pre-existing buyer contacts. These can inflate prices independent of intrinsic artistic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience taste is age- and experience-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Young audiences often prefer spectacle and entertainment (Barnum, pantomime) to 'subtle delicacies' of classical works; culture is an acquired taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators and educators should recognise that appreciation for certain arts develops over time; expect and accommodate differing ideals across age groups rather than assuming immediate acceptance of high art forms.
